subject: Ingress fabric decision for NimbleCloud private deployment: endpoint gateway vs tunnel
messages:
From: Rajiv Patel <rajiv@nimblecloud.com>
To: Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Wed, 1 Dec 2027 09:02:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Private deploy connectivity question

Jordan / Marissa —

Thanks again for the demo last week. We're close to internal approval for a private deployment of Redwood inside our AWS account, but the infra team has a few hard requirements and wants your recommendation on which connectivity approach to use for inference traffic: VPC peering, PrivateLink (interface endpoint), or a site-to-site VPN into our VPC.

Constraints:
- We run inference from multiple app VPCs across two regions (us-west-2 primary, us-east-1 DR).
- Outbound traffic needs fixed egress IPs for our WAF allowlist (control-plane and data-plane).
- We have a legacy on-prem DC that must reach the model endpoints during a phased migration.
- Throughput: up to 6 Gbps sustained, spikes to 12 Gbps.
- Security: mutual TLS preferred; we need clear auditability for SOC2.

Can you outline tradeoffs and a recommended pattern for a production rollout (including fallback for outages)? If you have a short one-pager or topology sketch that maps to these constraints, please attach.

Appreciate a concise recommendation — Rajiv
From: Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.ai>
To: Rajiv Patel <rajiv@nimblecloud.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Thu, 2 Dec 2027 10:18:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Private deploy connectivity question

Rajiv — thanks for the detail. High level recommendation upfront: a hybrid approach. Short summary (details below and attached one-pager):

Recommended baseline: PrivateLink (interface endpoints) for the Redwood data-plane + a managed site-to-site VPN for on-prem reachability and DR fallback.
Why:
- PrivateLink gives predictable per-connection interface endpoints, preserves service-level isolation across accounts, and allows per-AZ redundancy. It avoids exposing model endpoints on the public internet and gives you control over egress IPs via NAT in your VPCs.
- Peering offers lower latency and higher throughput but only works when Redwood is deployed inside the same cloud account / VPC space and is fragile when you have multiple accounts or overlapping IP ranges. Given you have multi-account VPCs and on-prem, peering is brittle at scale.
- VPN is necessary during migration and as a cross-cloud fallback; however, throughput and latency are weaker and jitter higher. Use it as a fallback path and for admin plane access, not primary real-time inference at full scale unless you terminate at a high-throughput virtual appliance.

Tradeoffs (quick):
- Latency: peering < PrivateLink (tens of ms vs low ms) — caveat: same-region peering can be sub-ms for co-located networks.
- Throughput: peering > PrivateLink per-connection; PrivateLink scales with ENIs and will incur per-ENI costs. VPN < both and depends on tunnel capacity.
- Security: PrivateLink keeps traffic inside AWS fabric between your VPC and Redwood-managed service endpoint; peering is L3 routing and requires tighter IP controls. VPN adds predictable encryption boundary but requires key/rotation ops.
- Operational: PrivateLink gives clearer per-service access controls and logging; peering requires route management and is harder to gate by service.

Suggested rollout:
1) Start with PrivateLink in primary region (us-west-2) for immediate secure access and egress IP control via a small NAT fleet.
2) Configure a managed S2S VPN into your on-prem DC for migration traffic and DR path to us-east-1.
3) If you later consolidate apps into a single AWS account and need sub-ms latency/very high throughput, evaluate peering for that specific VPC-to-VPC path and migrate progressively.

I've attached a short one-pager and a topology sketch. If you want, we can run a brief throughput test during POC to validate egress NAT sizing and PrivateLink ENI counts.

Next steps: schedule a 60-min tech workshop with your infra and security teams (I'd bring Ben C. and Kim P. from our solutions engineering). I'll follow up with times.

— Jordan

Attachment: redwood_ingress-options-onepager.pdf
From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>
To: Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.ai>, Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Sun, 5 Dec 2027 14:05:00 -0800
Subject: internal: NimbleCloud recommendation draft

Team — drafting the architecture to propose for Rajiv. Key points to land in the workshop:

1) Baseline topology (attached sketch): PrivateLink endpoints in us-west-2 fronted by a small NAT/egress pool so NimbleCloud can announce fixed egress IPs to their WAF vendor (they asked explicitly). We'll place endpoints in two AZs and autoscale the egress NAT instances behind an ALB.

2) VPN for on-prem: terminate two tunnels to a redundant virtual appliance (Transit Gateway or third-party appliance) with dynamic routing (BGP) so we can advertise prefixes and failover gracefully. Use IPsec AES-GCM and rotate PSKs or use certificate-based tunnels.

3) Peering only as an optimization: if they choose to move all app VPCs into the same account, we can propose a dedicated peering mesh for high-throughput low-latency apps. But note: peering will require CIDR remediation and extra route-table guardrails.

Operational concerns / Sizing:
- PrivateLink ENI limits: ensure ENI provisioning per AZ based on concurrent connections (we should estimate with the POC test).
- NAT sizing: 6 Gbps sustained -> consider autoscaling EC2 NAT or use a managed egress NAT gateway (cost vs throughput tradeoff).
- Observability: ensure VPC flow logs and PrivateLink endpoint logs are forwarded to their SIEM; Redwood will provide additional token-level traces.

Risks to call out: overlapping CIDRs (NimbleCloud has several /16s); if overlaps exist, PrivateLink is less impacted than peering. Also call out inter-region routing — PrivateLink today is regional; cross-region requires separate endpoints.

I attached the sketch and a brief POC scope (nimblecloud-poc-scope.docx). I'll be on the workshop to own sizing.

— Ben

Attachment: nimblecloud-poc-scope.docx
From: Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.ai>
To: Rajiv Patel <rajiv@nimblecloud.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>, Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>, contracts@nimblecloud.com
Date: Wed, 8 Dec 2027 15:14:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Private deploy connectivity question

Rajiv — appreciate the quick turnaround on constraints. We've consolidated our recommendation below and included explicit next steps so your infra and security teams can action.

Final recommendation (concise):
- Primary: AWS PrivateLink in us-west-2 (two AZs) with a fronting egress NAT pool for fixed egress IPs.
- Migration / fallback: Dual-terminated site-to-site VPN (BGP) to your on-prem DC.
- Optimization (optional): After account consolidation, evaluate targeted VPC peering for the small set of very latency-sensitive app VPCs.

Why this pattern for NimbleCloud: meets your egress IP requirement, minimizes attack surface (no public internet exposure), isolates service access per-account, and gives a straightforward operational rollback (VPN can carry traffic if PrivateLink ENIs need maintenance).

POC / Workshop agenda (60 mins):
1) Runbook review: NAT sizing, ENI provisioning, endpoint placement (15m)
2) Security & audit: mTLS termination, flow logs, IAM controls for endpoints (15m)
3) Connectivity test plan: throughput spike tests, failover to VPN, monitoring hooks (20m)
4) Next steps & ownership: sign-off, timeline, contracts (10m)

Attachments: nimblecloud-poc-scope.docx (scope + success criteria), redwood_ingress-options-onepager.pdf
Doc link: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1NimbleCloud-POC

Could you share a few times for the workshop and the name of the on-prem network owner (for VPN peering)? If helpful, we can include a short cost estimate for NAT vs managed gateway runs.

Thanks — Jordan
